meta.title: Who really said "He is suffering from delusions of adequacy"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Eisenhower. The earliest known instance is critic Walter Kerr's 18 Oct 1951 New York Herald Tribune review; in 1954 an MP aimed the jibe at Eisenhower.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'He is suffering from delusions of adequacy'?
meta.ogDescription: Walter Kerr wrote the earliest known instance, in a 1951 Broadway review. Eisenhower wasn't the author — in 1954 Michael Foot aimed the jibe at him.

answer.label: Not Dwight D. Eisenhower — actually Walter Kerr
answer.authorDates: 1913–1996 · drama critic, New York Herald Tribune
answer.sourceLine: Kerr wrote the earliest known instance on 18 October 1951, reviewing the Broadway show “Buy Me Blue Ribbons” for the New York Herald Tribune — Quote Investigator traces the coinage to him, calling this the earliest instance it located; the target was the play’s actor-producer, Jay Robinson. Eisenhower is attached to it only because in August 1954 the British Labour MP Michael Foot turned the phrase on the president — and said in the same breath that someone else had coined it.

source.heading: The review that first printed it

docMeta.dd: New York Herald Tribune, review of “Buy Me Blue Ribbons”
Walter Kerr, Pieces at Eight (Simon and Schuster, 1957), pp. 101–102

source.excerpt: All Mr. Robinson can honestly do now is to take his own advice. At the moment, he is suffering from delusions of adequacy.
trail: 18 October 1951 — Walter Kerr’s New York Herald Tribune notice of “Buy Me Blue Ribbons” carries the line. Quote Investigator transcribes it from page 20 and calls it the earliest instance it located ↗.
24 October 1951 — Variety repeats the jibe as the quip of the week, naming Kerr of the Herald Tribune and Jay Robinson as its target; the full issue is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗.

15 August 1954 — Michael Foot, then Labour MP for Plymouth Devonport, turns the phrase on President Eisenhower while attributing it to “someone,” as carried that day by the Daily Boston Globe and the Corpus Christi Caller-Times, per Quote Investigator’s transcript ↗.
1957 — Kerr reworks it for his own collection Pieces at Eight (Simon and Schuster, New York), pp. 101–102, as quoted by Quote Investigator ↗.

source.rightsNote: The wording was first published on 18 October 1951 in the New York Herald Tribune, and reprinted by Kerr in Pieces at Eight (Simon and Schuster, 1957) — both well after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff, so the text should be treated as in copyright rather than free to reuse at length. We have not traced who holds the rights today: the review’s first-publication proprietor was the Herald Tribune, the 1957 book was published by Simon and Schuster, and for a 1951 US work the renewal record would need checking too. Quoting the sentence with attribution is ordinary critical citation; reproducing the surrounding review is not.

author.name: Walter Kerr
author.heading: Who Walter Kerr was
author.metaLine: 1913–1996 · American drama critic · 1978 Pulitzer Prize for Criticism
author.bio: Walter Francis Kerr (1913–1996) became theater critic of the New York Herald Tribune in 1951 and held the job until the paper folded, writing notices sharp enough that rival papers quoted them back. He won the 1978 Pulitzer Prize for Criticism “for articles on the theater.” He was a playwright and director as well as a reviewer, which gave his verdicts on acting an insider’s precision — and is a large part of why a line like this one landed.

misattribution.heading: The Eisenhower problem
misattribution.intro: The Eisenhower credit is an inversion. He really is in this story — on the receiving end of it.

items.why: On 15 August 1954 the Labour MP Michael Foot used the phrase about Eisenhower — “He suffers, as someone has said, from delusions, of adequacy” — and that “as someone has said” is Foot disclaiming authorship outright. Quote Investigator transcribes the remark from the Daily Boston Globe ↗. The line also appears nowhere on Eisenhower’s own Wikiquote page ↗, in any section.

Aggregators circulate a flattened “He had delusions of adequacy” alongside the real thing. The 1951 review reads “he is suffering from delusions of adequacy,” and Kerr kept “suffering” when he rewrote it for his 1957 book. Sites that do carry the full wording credit Kerr correctly but name no source ↗.

In 1967 Heston applied the phrase to himself, saying he had delusions of adequacy as a conductor. It is one of a run of reuses catalogued by Quote Investigator ↗: Heston’s aside and a 1987 David Brin novel both drop the credit, loosening the line from the man who wrote it. Diana Rigg’s 1983 anthology No Turn Unstoned is the opposite case — a compilation of theatre reviews that reprints Kerr’s own 1957 sentence verbatim.

misattribution.truthLine: It is Walter Kerr’s, written on deadline in October 1951 about a Broadway show that lasted 13 performances — and in 1954 a British MP aimed it at a sitting US president. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Kerr was in his first year as the Herald Tribune’s theater critic when “Buy Me Blue Ribbons” opened at the Empire Theatre on 17 October 1951. Sumner Locke Elliott had written it, Cyril Ritchard directed, and its young star Jay Robinson had also produced it. The show closed after 13 performances, and Kerr’s notice supplied the epitaph.

What made the phrase travel is its economy: it borrows the shape of a clinical diagnosis — delusions of grandeur — and lets the air out. Wiktionary logs it as exactly that, an ironic variation on the older term. It did not stay on the theater pages either: by August 1954 a British MP was deploying it in remarks about the leadership of an American president.
context.detailsSummary: What happened to the actor, and where the line went next
detailsBody: The notice did not end Jay Robinson’s career. Robinson (1930–2013) was cast as Caligula in The Robe (1953) and again in Demetrius and the Gladiators (1954), then took roles in The Virgin Queen (1955), The Wild Party (1956) and My Man Godfrey (1957).

Kerr liked the line enough to keep it. He reworked it for Pieces at Eight, his 1957 Simon and Schuster collection, where it becomes a rhetorical question about what gameness is worth in a man suffering from delusions of adequacy. Quote Investigator follows the phrase onward through a 1967 Charlton Heston aside about his own conducting, Diana Rigg’s 1983 compilation No Turn Unstoned, and David Brin’s 1987 novel The Uplift War.
context.pull: Robinson survived it. The actor Kerr diagnosed went on to play Caligula in Hollywood — twice.
